summary.text: Lesson 2-4 of enVision Math Grade 4: the addition algorithm on greater numbers — four, five and six digits, three addends, alignment by place value, and estimates as the guard rail.

why.text: Same algorithm, higher stakes: with more columns there are more places for a carry to vanish, which is exactly why the estimate habit from 2-2 matters more here, not less.

objectives.text: Add numbers through six digits with the standard algorithm
Add three addends, choosing a helpful order
Align digits by place value and explain why it matters
Use an estimate to reject an unreasonable sum

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-4. Two things to watch: alignment (one question shows the left-edge error and its wildly wrong result) and finishing all three addends (the running total after two is a distractor on purpose). The mental-math questions are there to show the algorithm is not always the best tool, even at this size.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Write the estimate down before every exact answer.

cards.def:
**The addition algorithm does not change with size — more columns, same trades.**
• 24,595 + 19,255 works exactly like 358 + 277, just five columns wide.
• If it works for hundreds, it works for hundred thousands.

**Digits must be stacked by place value — ones under ones, tens under tens.**
• Adding 5,306 + 473 with left edges aligned adds the 4 hundreds as 4 thousands.
• Lining up the RIGHT edge does this automatically for whole numbers.
cards.hint: The ones digits anchor the whole stack. Start there.

cards.def:
**Add two numbers, then add the next to that running total — or pair friendly numbers first.**
• The Commutative and Associative Properties make any order legal.
• Watch for columns that pass 19: a carry can be 2.

**With big numbers, the estimate matters more, not less — mistakes grow with the columns.**
• 24,595 + 19,255: estimate 25,000 + 19,000 = 44,000 before touching the algorithm.
• An exact answer far from the estimate is guilty until proven innocent.

questions.q: Two towns count their recycling: 24,595 pounds and 19,255 pounds. What is the total?
questions.hint: Same algorithm as three-digit numbers — just more columns.

ex.main: **43,850.** Three carries, five columns, nothing new — just more of the same trades.
ex.tip: Check against the estimate: 25,000 + 19,000 = 44,000. The exact answer sits right beside it.

questions.hint: Work right to left, column by column.

ex.main: **63,895.** One early carry, then clean columns the rest of the way.
ex.tip: A zero inside a big number is just another digit — it takes the carry and passes the sum along.

questions.q: Before adding 24,595 + 19,255 exactly, you estimate by rounding each to the nearest thousand. Which estimate is right?
questions.hint: Round each number at the thousands place on its own merits.
steps: 24,595: the 5 in the hundreds rounds it UP to 25,000.
19,255: the 2 in the hundreds leaves it at 19,000.

ex.main: **44,000.** One number rounded up, one stayed — each on its own digit.
ex.tip: The wrong options each misround one number. Rounding is per-number, never a package deal.

questions.q: A city collects 30,283 pounds of paper, 63,423 pounds of glass, and 6,538 pounds of metal. What is the total?
questions.hint: Add two, then add the third to the running total.
steps: Three addends crossed into six digits — the algorithm did not blink.

ex.main: **100,244.** Two additions in a row, and the total crossed one hundred thousand.
ex.tip: The distractor 93,706 is the running total after two addends — finishing all three is the test of attention here.

questions.hint: This one carries in almost every column.
steps: Tens: 6 + 7 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1. Hundreds: 4 + 7 + 1 = 12. Write 2, carry 1.

ex.main: **87,245.** Four carries in a row — a good stress test of the trade routine.
ex.tip: Heavy-carry additions are where narrating each trade earns its keep. Rushing is how carries vanish.

questions.q: Adding 5,306 + 473, Marco lines the 4 of 473 under the 5 of 5,306 and gets 10,036. What went wrong?
opts: He lined up left edges instead of place values — 473 has no thousands, so its 4 belongs under the hundreds
questions.hint: What did the 4 of 473 get added to?
steps: Lined up by left edges, the 4 hundreds sat in the thousands column.
Marco really computed 5,306 + 4,730 — a different problem.
Right-edge alignment puts every whole-number digit in its true column automatically.

ex.main: **Misalignment — the true sum is 5,779.** His arithmetic was fine; his columns were lying to him.
ex.tip: A sum wildly bigger than both addends suggests digits sat in the wrong columns. The estimate (5,000 + 500) would have caught it.

questions.q: One stadium seats 68,745 people and another seats 25,899. How many seats do they hold together?
steps: Tens: 4 + 9 + 1 = 14. Write 4, carry 1. Hundreds: 7 + 8 + 1 = 16. Write 6, carry 1.

ex.main: **94,644.** Every column traded, and the estimate stood guard the whole way.
ex.tip: When every column carries, slow down on purpose. This is exactly where speed leaks digits.

questions.q: What is 49,999 + 50,001, and what is the FASTEST honest way to see it?
opts: 100,000 — move 1 from 50,001 to 49,999 and the problem becomes 50,000 + 50,000
100,000 — but only the full algorithm can be trusted
questions.hint: One addend is 1 short of round; the other is 1 over.
steps: Moving an amount between addends never changes a sum. That is lesson 2-1 working at scale.

ex.main: **100,000, by moving the 1 across.** Mental strategies do not expire when the numbers get big.
ex.tip: Before any big addition, spend three seconds looking for a reshape. Sometimes the algorithm never needs to show up.

questions.q: To add 9,875 + 12,125 + 30,000 quickly, which plan wins?
opts: Add 30,000 to 9,875 first because it is the biggest
Round everything to the nearest ten thousand and call the result exact
questions.hint: Two of these addends were made for each other.
steps: Look at the tails: 875 + 125 = 1,000. These two want to be paired.
Any order is legal — so choose the order that makes round numbers.

ex.main: **Pair the friendly two first: 52,000.** Order is a free choice; spend it where it pays.
ex.tip: Scan the endings before adding a list. Tails that sum to 1,000 are gifts, and they are common in real data.

questions.q: Jon claims 24,595 + 19,255 = 63,850. His estimate was 44,000. What should he conclude?
opts: The claim is about 20,000 past the estimate — recheck; the true sum is near 44,000
The estimate must be the wrong one
A bigger answer is safer, so keep 63,850
questions.hint: Measure the gap between claim and estimate first.
steps: Rounding error at the thousands place cannot produce a 20,000 gap.
So the exact work has a mistake — likely a phantom carry in the ten thousands.
Redone, the sum is 43,850, snug against the estimate.

ex.main: **Recheck the work — 43,850 is the real sum.** A 20,000 gap is a siren, not noise.
ex.tip: Trust the estimate exactly this far: it cannot find the error, but it can refuse to let a wrong answer through.
